message:
SITUATION:
Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
The new supplier's resin caused the rise in defects.

RESPONSE:
Not from this information, and I don't think either of you can either. Three changes started in the same week, so the timing fits each of them equally well. That leaves both explanations as reasonable guesses, not conclusions. The good news is that you can probably settle it within days using data you already have, plus one simple test.

## Why neither conclusion follows yet

- **The new resin.** This is the only change that lines up with the timing, and three things changed at once.
- **The night crew.** Identical specs don't rule out the resin. Specs cover nominal properties, but lots can still differ in:
  - moisture content when they arrive
  - how readily the pellets absorb moisture
  - additive packages
  - lot-to-lot consistency
  - contamination
- **Humidity and resin together.** These two can interact. If the new resin absorbs moisture more readily, or arrives wetter, hot and humid weather would expose it while your old resin coped. In that case the actual fix might be your drying process, not the supplier contract.

## How to separate them

**1. Split the defect rate by shift.** If the night crew is the cause, night-shift defects should have risen while day-shift defects stayed near 1.1%. If both shifts rose about equally, the crew is unlikely to be the main cause.

**2. Split by resin.** If any old-supplier stock was still being used after the switch, compare defect rates on old versus new resin over the same weeks. If none is left, check whether defects vary between lots of the new resin.

**3. Plot daily defect rate against humidity.** If humidity is driving it, defects should rise and fall with humid days on both shifts and both resins. Night-time humidity often differs from daytime humidity, so record it by shift if you can.

**4. Look at which types of defect increased.** The defect type often points to the cause:

| Defect type | Usually suggests |
|---|---|
| Splay, silver streaks, bubbles, brittleness | Moisture: resin drying or humidity |
| Black specks, contamination, colour variation | Resin quality |
| Short shots, flash, sink marks, inconsistent dimensions | Process settings or operator handling |

**5. Check your resin dryers.** Look at dryer temperature, residence time and, if you measure it, dew point. Measure the moisture content of the new resin just before moulding. If it's above the processing limit, you've likely found the cause.

**6. Run a short controlled test.** If you can get some of the old resin, run it alongside the new resin on the same machine, same shift and same day. If not, run the new resin under tightly controlled drying. A few runs of this will tell you more than weeks of arguing.

Also check whether 1.1% to 1.9% is a real shift and not normal variation. At typical moulding volumes it almost certainly is, but it only takes a moment to confirm against your weekly history.

## On the decisions

- **Hold off on cancelling the contract** until steps 1–5 point clearly at the resin. If the cause turns out to be humidity or drying, switching suppliers won't fix it, and you'll have paid for the switch anyway.
- **Hold off on blaming the night crew** for the same reason. If the shift split doesn't support it, that conclusion would be unfair to them and wouldn't fix the problem.

It's also quite possible that more than one factor is at work. For example, an inexperienced crew may be less likely to notice resin that isn't drying properly on humid nights. The breakdowns above will show that too.
